newsitem.title: USA: FBI lab problems do not jeopardize cases - Freeh.
newsitem.headline: FBI lab problems do not jeopardize cases - Freeh.

text.p: FBI Director Louis Freeh said Wednesday that problems at the bureau's laboratory will not jeopardise any pending bureau criminal cases.
"Despite serious problems in our lab, I know of no FBI case that will be compromised by those issues," Freeh said at a House Appropriations subcommittee hearing.

An investigation by the Justice Department's inspector general has sharply criticised the laboratory for poor management practices and sloppy handling of evidence and raised questions about procedures and contaminated evidence. A final report on the lab is due soon.

In January, the Federal Bureau of Investigation announced it had suspended four officials from the unit in response to the investigation, including a whistleblower whose initial complaints triggered the inquiry.

Last month, the Justice Department told about 50 prosecutors nationwide about problems at the FBI crime laboratory that could affect their cases, and there have been concerns that the trial in the 1993 Oklahoma City federal building bombing, scheduled to begin March 31 in Denver, could be affected.
Freeh said he was taking a number of steps to solve the problems at the lab and was looking for someone with outstanding scientific credentials to be its director.

Republicans on the panel said they were losing confidence in Freeh and the FBI and feared political concerns were compromising the bureau's independence. They said they were especially upset about the unauthorised delivery of FBI files on about 1,000 individuals to the White House in 1993.
"The leadership of the FBI has brought the whole operation into question and you are the leader," Representative Bob Livingston of Louisiana told Freeh.
"I'm watching political agendas creep into the department and the FBI. It's extremely troubling," Representative Hal Rogers of Kentucky added.
Freeh called the release of the files "a terrible violation of privacy," but said procedures have been put in place to prevent the misuse of files.
"My independence and my integrity as FBI director is the most important thing to me," Freeh said.

Freeh separately named Michael DeFeo, a senior Justice Department official, to be assistant FBI director in charge of the agency's Office of Professional Responsibility to investigate allegations against FBI agents and employees.
